title: Manual Muscle Testing (MMT)
keywords: mmt manual muscle test testing strength grading oxford scale kendall daniels worthingham muscle power taqat
summary: Grade strength from 0 to 5 like an expert: positions, stabilisation, resistance, gravity-minimised testing and substitutions for 46 muscle tests.
ur: Muscle strength ko 0 se 5 tak grade karna — sahi position, stabilisation, resistance aur substitutions ke saath.

sources.title: Avers & Brown — Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing (10th ed.)

goals.beginner: Know what each grade means and why gravity decides grade 3.
goals.intermediate: Test any muscle with the right position, stabilisation and resistance.
goals.advanced: Grade 0–2 and +/− grades; catch every substitution.
goals.expert: Read weakness patterns (root, nerve, UMN, muscle) and pass OSCE stations.

concepts.title: What manual muscle testing measures
concepts.body: MMT tells you how much force a **muscle group** can produce compared with gravity and with your resistance. It is quick, needs no equipment and is the language every physiotherapist, doctor and examiner understands.
bullets: Use it to find weakness, compare sides, track recovery and decide on exercise.
It grades **voluntary strength** — it assumes normal tone and the ability to follow commands.
It is a **screen**, not a precise measure: grades 4 and 5 are subjective.
concepts.ur: MMT se pata chalta hai ke muscle gravity aur aap ki resistance ke against kitni strength laga sakta hai — dono sides compare karein.

concepts.title: The 0–5 scale (Oxford / MRC)
concepts.body: Every grade is defined by two questions: **does the part move through full range against gravity?** and **how much resistance can it hold?**

head: Grade
Name
What you see
rows: Full range against gravity, holds maximal resistance
Full range against gravity, holds moderate resistance, yields to maximal
Full range against gravity, no added resistance
Contraction felt or seen, no joint movement

concepts.ur: Grade 3 woh line hai jahan muscle bina resistance ke gravity ke against full range kar le. Us se upar resistance, neeche gravity-minimised position.

concepts.title: Gravity decides grade 3
concepts.body: Grade 3 is the pivot. First ask the patient to move through range **against gravity** with no resistance. If they can, you go up (add resistance for 4 and 5). If they can't, you go down: reposition so the movement happens in the **horizontal plane** (gravity minimised) for grades 2, 1 and 0.
concepts.ur: Pehle against gravity test karein. Ho jaye to resistance add karein, na ho to position change kar ke horizontal plane mein test karein.

concepts.title: Make test vs break test
concepts.body: In a **break test** (the usual MMT method) the patient holds the end of the test range and you gradually push to 'break' the hold: “Hold — don't let me move you.” In a **make test** the patient pushes into your still hand. Break tests give higher, more discriminating grades; whichever you use, use it consistently and document it.
concepts.ur: Break test mein patient hold karta hai aur aap dheere dheere push karte hain; make test mein patient aap ke hand ko push karta hai.

concepts.title: The universal 8-step sequence
concepts.body: Every MMT follows the same order — learn it once and it works for any muscle.
bullets: **Explain** and get consent; ask about pain.
**Position** the patient for the test (against gravity first).
**Stabilise** the proximal segment.
**Demonstrate** or move the part passively through range to show the movement and check range.
**Test grade 3**: patient moves through range against gravity.
**Resist** gradually (2–3 seconds) at the distal end of the segment.
**Grade** — and compare with the other side.
**Document** side, movement, grade and any pain or substitution.

concepts.title: When not to resist
concepts.body: Resisted testing loads bones, joints and the cardiovascular system.
bullets: Avoid resistance over an **unhealed fracture**, after **recent surgery** (follow the protocol) or with **acute inflammation**.
Teach breathing out during effort — strong holding can trigger a **Valsalva** response (caution in cardiac or hypertensive patients).
Be gentle with **osteoporosis** and avoid loaded trunk flexion.
Stop and document if the test reproduces significant **pain**.

concepts.title: Stabilise the proximal segment
concepts.body: Stabilisation fixes the bone the muscle pulls **from**, so only the tested movement happens. Good stabilisation is the difference between testing gluteus medius and testing a patient who hikes the hip.
bullets: Stabilise close to the joint, on the proximal segment.
Use a firm, comfortable hand; the patient can also hold the table.
Never stabilise on a painful area.
concepts.ur: Jahan se muscle start hota hai us part ko firmly stabilise karein taake doosre muscles help na kar saken.

concepts.title: Resistance: where, which way, how fast
concepts.body: Apply resistance at the **distal end of the moving segment** (long lever) but **never across a second joint**. Push in the direction **opposite** to the muscle's pull, building up smoothly over 2–3 seconds and holding — no sudden jerks.
concepts.ur: Resistance hamesha moving segment ke distal end par, muscle ki pull ke opposite direction mein, dheere dheere 2–3 seconds mein dein.

concepts.title: Group tests by position
concepts.body: Plan the examination so the patient changes position as little as possible: do all **sitting** tests, then **supine**, **side-lying** and **prone**. A full lower-limb screen takes minutes when grouped well.

head: Position
Common tests
rows: Shoulder flexion/abduction, elbow, wrist, hip flexion, knee extension, hip rotation
Neck & trunk flexion, horizontal adduction, gravity-minimised hip tests
Hip abduction/adduction, gravity-minimised knee & shoulder tests
Neck & trunk extension, scapular muscles, shoulder extension/rotation, hip extension, knee flexion

concepts.title: Document like a professional
concepts.body: Write the side, movement (or muscle), grade and anything that changes interpretation. Example: **“R shoulder abduction 4/5, pain at end range; L 5/5. Break test, sitting.”** A table of both sides lets anyone see the pattern at a glance.

concepts.title: Plus and minus grades
concepts.body: Many clinics refine the scale with + and −. Definitions differ between textbooks, so state the convention you use. A widely taught one:

head: Grade
Meaning
rows: Full range against gravity, holds minimal resistance
More than half, but not all, of the range against gravity
Less than half of the range against gravity (initiates the movement)

concepts.ur: Plus/minus grades har book mein thore different hain — apni report mein likhein ke kaun sa system use kiya.

concepts.title: Catching substitutions
concepts.body: A weak muscle 'borrows' help. Watch the whole body, not just the limb.
bullets: **Shrugging** during shoulder flexion/abduction = upper trapezius.
**Leg drifting forward** in hip abduction = TFL/hip flexors.
**Fingers moving first** in wrist tests = long finger muscles.
**Tenodesis**: wrist extension passively closes the fingers; wrist flexion opens them.
**Momentum, leaning and holding the breath** to cheat any test.

concepts.title: Grades 2, 1 and 0 in practice
concepts.body: Gravity-minimised positions move the part in the horizontal plane: side-lying for sagittal-plane movements, supine or prone for frontal-plane movements. Support the limb (a smooth board or powder board helps). If there is no movement, **palpate** the muscle or tendon while the patient tries — a flicker is grade 1.

concepts.title: How reliable is MMT?
concepts.body: Agreement between testers is good for grades 0–3 and poor for 4 versus 5: a strong examiner can't 'break' a strong patient, so moderate weakness hides at grade 5. When strength matters (return to sport, research), use a **handheld dynamometer** or functional tests such as 30-second sit-to-stand or single-leg heel raises.

concepts.title: Read the pattern of weakness
concepts.body: Single grades matter less than the **pattern** across muscles.

head: Pattern
Suggests
rows: Muscles sharing one root (e.g. deltoid, biceps — C5)
Muscles sharing one nerve (e.g. deltoid + teres minor)
Arm extensors and leg flexors weaker, high tone, brisk reflexes

concepts.ur: Sirf ek muscle nahi, poora pattern dekhein: root, nerve, UMN, muscle ya junction.

concepts.title: When MMT is the wrong tool
concepts.body: MMT assumes isolated voluntary control. In **spasticity** (stroke, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy) describe tone, selective motor control and function instead. In young children, cognitive impairment or severe pain, use observation and functional tasks. Strong-but-painful versus weak-and-painless findings also guide diagnosis (contractile lesion vs neurological weakness).

concepts.title: MMT inside the ISNCSCI exam
concepts.body: The spinal cord injury standard grades **10 key muscles per side** (C5–T1, L2–S1) from 0 to 5, giving an upper-limb, lower-limb and total motor score (maximum 100). The same rules apply — supine testing, standard positions and grading.
bullets: C5 elbow flexors · C6 wrist extensors · C7 elbow extensors · C8 finger flexors (middle finger FDP) · T1 little-finger abductors
L2 hip flexors · L3 knee extensors · L4 ankle dorsiflexors · L5 long toe extensors · S1 ankle plantarflexors

questions.prompt: Where should resistance be applied?
options: At the distal end of the moving segment, without crossing another joint
On the proximal segment
Directly over the joint axis
Anywhere the patient finds comfortable
questions.explain: A distal point gives a long lever; crossing a second joint brings other muscles into the test.

questions.prompt: The main purpose of stabilisation is to…

Measure the joint angle
Increase the range of movement

stations.title: Grade hip abduction (gluteus medius)
stations.scenario: A 45-year-old with lateral hip pain shows a positive Trendelenburg sign on the right. Test and grade right hip abduction, then report your finding to the examiner.
tasks: Introduce yourself, explain the test and screen for pain.
Test and grade right hip abduction, comparing with the left.
Report the grade and any substitution.
checklist: Explains the test and obtains consent; asks about pain
Side-lying on the left, lower leg bent, right hip slightly extended in neutral rotation
Stabilises the iliac crest
Asks for full range against gravity before resisting (grade 3 check)
Applies resistance at the lateral distal thigh, building over 2–3 s
Spots and corrects hip flexion (TFL) or hip hiking
Compares with the other side
Reports side, grade and pain, e.g. “R hip abduction 4/5, pain-free; L 5/5”

stations.title: Grade elbow flexion below grade 3

Supports the limb on a smooth surface
Grades 2 if full range gravity-minimised, 2− if partial
Palpates the biceps tendon for a flicker when no movement occurs (grade 1 vs 0)
Documents grade and test position

stations.title: Upper-limb strength screen

Tests both sides

Recommends dermatome and reflex testing to confirm

cards.back: Prone, hand resting on the small of the back (shoulder internally rotated). Patient lifts the hand off the back, adducting and downwardly rotating the scapula.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Scapular adduction & downward rotation?
cards.back: Opposite side of the upper thorax.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Scapular adduction & downward rotation?
cards.back: On the medial border of the scapula/distal humerus, pushing toward abduction and upward rotation.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Scapular adduction & downward rotation (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Sitting, hand behind the back: patient draws the scapula toward the spine with the arm supported.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Scapular adduction & downward rotation?
cards.back: Along the medial border of the scapula, deep to the trapezius.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Scapular adduction & downward rotation?
cards.back: Middle trapezius (no downward rotation) and posterior deltoid/elbow extension lifting the hand.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Shoulder flexion?
cards.back: Anterior deltoid, coracobrachialis

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Shoulder flexion?
cards.back: Axillary nerve (C5–C6); coracobrachialis: musculocutaneous (C5–C7)

cards.front: Test position for Shoulder flexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, arm at the side, elbow slightly flexed, palm facing down. Patient raises the arm forward to 90°.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Shoulder flexion?
cards.back: Over the top of the shoulder (scapula/clavicle) to prevent shrugging.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Shoulder flexion?
cards.back: On the distal humerus just above the elbow, pushing down.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Shoulder flexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Side-lying on the untested side, arm supported on a smooth surface: patient slides the arm forward into flexion.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Shoulder flexion?
cards.back: Anterior deltoid over the front of the shoulder, just below the clavicle.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Shoulder flexion?
cards.back: Shrugging (upper trapezius), leaning back, biceps (elbow bends, shoulder rotates out).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Shoulder extension?
cards.back: Latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Shoulder extension?
cards.back: Thoracodorsal (C6–C8), lower subscapular (C5–C6), axillary (C5–C6)

cards.front: Test position for Shoulder extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Prone, arm at the side, internally rotated (palm up). Patient lifts the arm toward the ceiling.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Shoulder extension?
cards.back: Over the scapula.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Shoulder extension?
cards.back: On the back of the distal humerus, pushing down toward the table.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Shoulder extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Side-lying on the untested side, arm supported: patient slides the arm back into extension.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Shoulder extension?
cards.back: Latissimus dorsi and teres major at the posterior axillary fold; posterior deltoid behind the shoulder.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Shoulder extension?
cards.back: Scapular elevation/downward rotation and elbow flexion.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Shoulder abduction?
cards.back: Middle deltoid, supraspinatus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Shoulder abduction?
cards.back: Axillary (C5–C6); supraspinatus: suprascapular (C5–C6)

cards.front: Test position for Shoulder abduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, arm at the side, elbow slightly flexed, palm down. Patient lifts the arm out to the side to 90°.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Shoulder abduction?
cards.back: Over the top of the shoulder to prevent shrugging.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Shoulder abduction?
cards.back: On the distal humerus just above the elbow, pushing down toward adduction.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Shoulder abduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Supine, arm at the side on the table: patient slides the arm out into abduction.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Shoulder abduction?
cards.back: Middle deltoid over the lateral shoulder; supraspinatus above the spine of the scapula.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Shoulder abduction?
cards.back: Upper trapezius (hiking), lateral trunk lean, biceps (rotating out, then flexing).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Shoulder horizontal abduction?
cards.back: Posterior deltoid

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Shoulder horizontal abduction?
cards.back: Axillary nerve (C5–C6)

cards.front: Test position for Shoulder horizontal abduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Prone, shoulder abducted 90° with the arm over the edge of the table, elbow flexed 90°. Patient lifts the arm toward the ceiling.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Shoulder horizontal abduction?
cards.back: Over the scapula.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Shoulder horizontal abduction?
cards.back: On the back of the distal humerus, pushing down toward the floor.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Shoulder horizontal abduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Sitting, arm supported on a table at 90° flexion: patient moves the arm out horizontally.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Shoulder horizontal abduction?
cards.back: Posterior deltoid behind the shoulder, below the spine of the scapula.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Shoulder horizontal abduction?
cards.back: Rhomboids/middle trapezius (the scapula moves first) and the long head of triceps.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Shoulder horizontal adduction?
cards.back: Pectoralis major

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Shoulder horizontal adduction?
cards.back: Medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Shoulder horizontal adduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Supine, shoulder abducted 90°, elbow flexed 90°. Patient brings the arm across the chest.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Shoulder horizontal adduction?
cards.back: On the opposite shoulder.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Shoulder horizontal adduction?
cards.back: On the front of the distal humerus, pulling out toward horizontal abduction.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Shoulder horizontal adduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Sitting, arm supported on a table at 90° abduction: patient slides the arm forward across the table.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Shoulder horizontal adduction?
cards.back: Anterior axillary fold.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Shoulder horizontal adduction?
cards.back: Anterior deltoid, scapular protraction and trunk rotation.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Shoulder external rotation?
cards.back: Infraspinatus, teres minor

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Shoulder external rotation?
cards.back: Suprascapular (C5–C6); teres minor: axillary (C5–C6)

cards.front: Test position for Shoulder external rotation against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Prone, shoulder abducted 90°, elbow flexed 90° with the forearm hanging over the edge (towel under the humerus). Patient rotates the forearm up toward the head.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Shoulder external rotation?
cards.back: Under the distal humerus on the towel, keeping the arm in place.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Shoulder external rotation?
cards.back: On the distal forearm just above the wrist, pushing down toward internal rotation.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Shoulder external rotation (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Prone with the whole arm hanging over the edge: patient rotates the arm outward.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Shoulder external rotation?
cards.back: Infraspinatus below the spine of the scapula; teres minor along the lateral border.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Shoulder external rotation?
cards.back: Elbow extension (triceps) and scapular adduction/depression.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Shoulder internal rotation?
cards.back: Subscapularis (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major assist)

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Shoulder internal rotation?
cards.back: Upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5–C6)

cards.front: Test position for Shoulder internal rotation against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Prone, shoulder abducted 90°, elbow flexed 90°, forearm hanging over the edge. Patient rotates the forearm backward and up toward the ceiling.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Shoulder internal rotation?
cards.back: Under the distal humerus on the towel.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Shoulder internal rotation?
cards.back: On the distal forearm, pushing toward external rotation.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Shoulder internal rotation (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Prone with the whole arm hanging over the edge: patient rotates the arm inward.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Shoulder internal rotation?
cards.back: Subscapularis is deep — partly palpable in the posterior axilla.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Shoulder internal rotation?
cards.back: Scapular protraction/elevation and elbow extension.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Elbow flexion?
cards.back: Biceps brachii, brachialis, brachioradialis

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Elbow flexion?
cards.back: Musculocutaneous (C5–C6); brachioradialis: radial (C5–C6)

cards.front: Test position for Elbow flexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, arm at the side. Forearm supinated for biceps, pronated for brachialis, mid-position for brachioradialis. Patient bends the elbow.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Elbow flexion?
cards.back: Under the distal humerus / front of the shoulder.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Elbow flexion?
cards.back: On the distal forearm, pulling toward extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Elbow flexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Sitting with the arm supported at 90° abduction on a table (or side-lying): patient slides the forearm into flexion.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Elbow flexion?
cards.back: Biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa; brachioradialis on the lateral forearm.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Elbow flexion?
cards.back: Wrist flexors (the wrist flexes first) and shoulder flexion/trunk lean.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Elbow extension?
cards.back: Triceps brachii (anconeus)

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Elbow extension?
cards.back: Radial nerve (C6–C8, mainly C7)

cards.front: Test position for Elbow extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Prone, shoulder abducted 90° on the table, forearm hanging over the edge. Patient straightens the elbow (without locking it).

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Elbow extension?
cards.back: Under the distal humerus.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Elbow extension?
cards.back: On the back of the distal forearm, pushing toward flexion — just short of full extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Elbow extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Sitting, arm supported at 90° abduction on a table, elbow flexed: patient slides the forearm into extension.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Elbow extension?
cards.back: Triceps on the back of the arm just above the olecranon.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Elbow extension?
cards.back: Shoulder external rotation (letting gravity extend the elbow) and locking the elbow.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Forearm supination?
cards.back: Supinator, biceps brachii

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Forearm supination?
cards.back: Supinator: posterior interosseous/radial (C5–C6); biceps: musculocutaneous (C5–C6)

cards.front: Test position for Forearm supination against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, arm at the side, elbow flexed 90°, forearm pronated. Patient turns the palm up.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Forearm supination?
cards.back: Distal humerus, elbow against the side.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Forearm supination?
cards.back: Hand around the distal forearm, turning it toward pronation.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Forearm supination (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Shoulder flexed 90° with the elbow resting on the table, forearm vertical: patient turns the palm toward the face.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Forearm supination?
cards.back: Supinator over the back of the proximal radius; biceps tendon at the elbow.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Forearm supination?
cards.back: Shoulder external rotation/adduction and wrist extension.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Forearm pronation?
cards.back: Pronator teres, pronator quadratus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Forearm pronation?
cards.back: Median nerve (C6–C7); pronator quadratus: anterior interosseous (C8–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Forearm pronation against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, elbow flexed 90°, forearm supinated. Patient turns the palm down.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Forearm pronation?
cards.back: Distal humerus, elbow at the side.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Forearm pronation?
cards.back: Hand around the distal forearm, turning it toward supination.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Forearm pronation (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Shoulder flexed 90°, elbow on the table, forearm vertical: patient turns the palm away from the face.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Forearm pronation?
cards.back: Pronator teres on the proximal front of the forearm, medial to the biceps tendon.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Forearm pronation?
cards.back: Shoulder internal rotation/abduction and wrist flexion.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Wrist flexion?
cards.back: Flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Wrist flexion?
cards.back: FCR: median (C6–C7); FCU: ulnar (C7–C8)

cards.front: Test position for Wrist flexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm supinated and resting on the table, fingers relaxed. Patient bends the wrist up.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Wrist flexion?
cards.back: Front of the forearm just above the wrist.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Wrist flexion?
cards.back: On the palm over the metacarpal heads, pushing toward extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Wrist flexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Forearm in mid-position (ulnar border on the table): patient flexes the wrist sideways along the table.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Wrist flexion?
cards.back: FCR tendon lateral to palmaris longus; FCU tendon just above the pisiform.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Wrist flexion?
cards.back: Finger flexors (the fingers curl first).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Wrist extension?
cards.back: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Wrist extension?
cards.back: ECRL/ECRB: radial (C6–C7); ECU: posterior interosseous (C7–C8)

cards.front: Test position for Wrist extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm pronated and resting on the table, fingers relaxed. Patient lifts the hand up (extends the wrist).

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Wrist extension?
cards.back: Under the distal forearm.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Wrist extension?
cards.back: On the back of the hand over the metacarpals, pushing toward flexion.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Wrist extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Forearm in mid-position on the table: patient extends the wrist sideways along the table.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Wrist extension?
cards.back: ECRL/ECRB tendons at the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals; ECU beside the ulnar head.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Wrist extension?
cards.back: Finger extensors (the fingers straighten first).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Finger MCP flexion with IP extension?
cards.back: Lumbricals (with interossei)

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Finger MCP flexion with IP extension?
cards.back: Lumbricals 1–2: median (C8–T1); 3–4 and interossei: ulnar (C8–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Finger MCP flexion with IP extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm supinated, wrist neutral. Patient bends the knuckles (MCP joints) while keeping the fingers straight — a 'table-top' hand.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Finger MCP flexion with IP extension?
cards.back: Metacarpals in the palm.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Finger MCP flexion with IP extension?
cards.back: Under the proximal phalanges, pushing toward MCP extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Finger MCP flexion with IP extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Gravity has little effect on finger muscles: grade 2/1/0 by the range achieved and palpation.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Finger MCP flexion with IP extension?
cards.back: Lumbricals are not reliably palpable; feel the first dorsal interosseous in the first web space.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Finger MCP flexion with IP extension?
cards.back: Long finger flexors (the IP joints bend — a claw pattern).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Finger PIP flexion?
cards.back: Flexor digitorum superficialis

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Finger PIP flexion?
cards.back: Median nerve (C7–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Finger PIP flexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm supinated, wrist neutral; hold the other fingers straight (this blocks FDP). Patient bends the middle (PIP) joint while the fingertip stays loose.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Finger PIP flexion?
cards.back: Proximal phalanx of the tested finger, other fingers held in extension.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Finger PIP flexion?
cards.back: On the middle phalanx, pushing toward extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Finger PIP flexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range and palpation (gravity has little effect).

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Finger PIP flexion?
cards.back: FDS tendons at the front of the wrist, between palmaris longus and FCU.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Finger PIP flexion?
cards.back: FDP (the fingertip bends too) and wrist extension tenodesis.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Finger DIP flexion?
cards.back: Flexor digitorum profundus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Finger DIP flexion?
cards.back: Index/middle: anterior interosseous (median, C8–T1); ring/little: ulnar (C8–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Finger DIP flexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm supinated, wrist neutral. Hold the middle phalanx; patient bends the fingertip (DIP joint).

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Finger DIP flexion?
cards.back: Middle phalanx of the tested finger.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Finger DIP flexion?
cards.back: On the pad of the distal phalanx, pushing toward extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Finger DIP flexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range and palpation.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Finger DIP flexion?
cards.back: Front of the middle phalanx.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Finger DIP flexion?
cards.back: Wrist extension tenodesis (passive finger flexion).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Finger MCP extension?
cards.back: Extensor digitorum (extensor indicis, extensor digiti minimi)

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Finger MCP extension?
cards.back: Posterior interosseous nerve, radial (C7–C8)

cards.front: Test position for Finger MCP extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm pronated, wrist neutral, MCP and IP joints flexed. Patient straightens the knuckles (MCP joints).

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Finger MCP extension?
cards.back: Metacarpals/wrist.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Finger MCP extension?
cards.back: On the back of the proximal phalanges, pushing toward MCP flexion.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Finger MCP extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range and palpation.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Finger MCP extension?
cards.back: Extensor tendons over the back of the hand.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Finger MCP extension?
cards.back: Wrist flexion (tenodesis straightens the fingers).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Finger abduction?
cards.back: Dorsal interossei, abductor digiti minimi

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Finger abduction?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve (C8–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Finger abduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm pronated, fingers straight and together. Patient spreads the fingers apart.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Finger abduction?
cards.back: Wrist and metacarpals.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Finger abduction?
cards.back: On the side of each proximal phalanx, pushing toward adduction (test one finger at a time).

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Finger abduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range and palpation.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Finger abduction?
cards.back: First dorsal interosseous in the first web space; abductor digiti minimi on the ulnar border of the hand.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Finger abduction?
cards.back: Finger extension (extensor digitorum spreads the fingers slightly).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Finger adduction?
cards.back: Palmar interossei

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Finger adduction?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve (C8–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Finger adduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm pronated, fingers spread. Patient brings each finger in toward the middle finger.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Finger adduction?
cards.back: Metacarpals.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Finger adduction?
cards.back: Pull the finger away from the middle finger (into abduction).

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Finger adduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Finger adduction?
cards.back: Not reliably palpable (deep in the hand).

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Finger adduction?
cards.back: Finger flexion (the long flexors pull the fingers together).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Thumb palmar abduction?
cards.back: Abductor pollicis brevis (abductor pollicis longus assists)

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Thumb palmar abduction?
cards.back: APB: median, recurrent branch (C8–T1); APL: posterior interosseous (C7–C8)

cards.front: Test position for Thumb palmar abduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm supinated, thumb relaxed. Patient lifts the thumb straight up, away from the palm.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Thumb palmar abduction?
cards.back: Metacarpals and wrist.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Thumb palmar abduction?
cards.back: On the lateral proximal phalanx, pushing toward adduction.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Thumb palmar abduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range and palpation.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Thumb palmar abduction?
cards.back: Lateral thenar eminence.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Thumb palmar abduction?
cards.back: Abductor pollicis longus (the thumb moves toward the radial side instead).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Thumb opposition?
cards.back: Opponens pollicis (with APB and flexor pollicis brevis)

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Thumb opposition?
cards.back: Median nerve, recurrent branch (C8–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Thumb opposition against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm supinated. Patient brings the pad of the thumb to the pad of the little finger.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Thumb opposition?
cards.back: Hand and metacarpals.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Thumb opposition?
cards.back: On the thumb metacarpal, rotating it back toward the plane of the palm.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Thumb opposition (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Thumb opposition?
cards.back: Lateral border of the thumb metacarpal.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Thumb opposition?
cards.back: Flexor pollicis longus and APB (flexion or abduction without rotation).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Thumb adduction?
cards.back: Adductor pollicis

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Thumb adduction?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve, deep branch (C8–T1)

cards.front: Test position for Thumb adduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Forearm pronated, thumb abducted. Patient brings the thumb against the side of the hand.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Thumb adduction?
cards.back: Metacarpals.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Thumb adduction?
cards.back: On the medial proximal phalanx of the thumb, pulling into abduction.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Thumb adduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Thumb adduction?
cards.back: First web space, palmar side.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Thumb adduction?
cards.back: Flexor pollicis longus — Froment's sign (the thumb tip bends when pinching paper).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Hip flexion?
cards.back: Iliopsoas (psoas major, iliacus)

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Hip flexion?
cards.back: Femoral (L2–L3) for iliacus; lumbar plexus L1–L3 for psoas

cards.front: Test position for Hip flexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, thighs on the table, knees bent over the edge, hands holding the table. Patient lifts the thigh off the table.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Hip flexion?
cards.back: On the iliac crest or top of the shoulder on the same side.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Hip flexion?
cards.back: On the distal thigh just above the knee, pushing down toward extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Hip flexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Side-lying on the untested side, test leg supported: patient slides the hip into flexion (knee bent).

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Hip flexion?
cards.back: Psoas tendon just below the inguinal ligament, medial to sartorius.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Hip flexion?
cards.back: Sartorius (the hip rotates out and abducts), TFL (rotates in and abducts), leaning back.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Hip extension?
cards.back: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Hip extension?
cards.back: Inferior gluteal (L5–S2); hamstrings: sciatic (L5–S2)

cards.front: Test position for Hip extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Prone, knee straight (gluteus maximus + hamstrings) — or knee bent 90° to isolate gluteus maximus. Patient lifts the leg toward the ceiling.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Hip extension?
cards.back: Over the pelvis (PSIS area).

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Hip extension?
cards.back: On the back of the distal thigh, above the knee, pushing down.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Hip extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Side-lying on the untested side, leg supported: patient extends the hip.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Hip extension?
cards.back: Gluteus maximus over the buttock; hamstring tendons behind the knee.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Hip extension?
cards.back: Lumbar extension and pelvic rotation (the back arches).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Hip abduction?
cards.back: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Hip abduction?
cards.back: Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)

cards.front: Test position for Hip abduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Side-lying on the untested side, lower leg bent for balance, test hip slightly extended. Patient lifts the leg up without rolling back.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Hip abduction?
cards.back: On the iliac crest to stop hip hiking and rolling.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Hip abduction?
cards.back: On the lateral distal thigh (or above the ankle), pushing down toward adduction.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Hip abduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Supine: patient slides the leg out to the side.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Hip abduction?
cards.back: Gluteus medius just below the iliac crest, above the greater trochanter.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Hip abduction?
cards.back: Hip flexion (TFL — the leg drifts forward), hip hiking (quadratus lumborum), rolling backward.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Hip adduction?
cards.back: Adductor magnus, longus and brevis, gracilis, pectineus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Hip adduction?
cards.back: Obturator (L2–L4); adductor magnus also tibial part of sciatic (L4)

cards.front: Test position for Hip adduction against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Side-lying on the test side, top leg held in about 25° abduction by the therapist. Patient lifts the bottom leg up to meet the top leg.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Hip adduction?
cards.back: Therapist supports the top leg; the patient holds the table.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Hip adduction?
cards.back: On the medial distal thigh of the bottom leg, pushing down.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Hip adduction (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Supine, leg abducted: patient slides the leg back toward the midline.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Hip adduction?
cards.back: Adductor tendons in the medial groin.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Hip adduction?
cards.back: Hip flexion (pectineus and hip flexors) and pelvic tilt.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Obturators, gemelli, quadratus femoris, piriformis, gluteus maximus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Nerves to obturator internus and quadratus femoris (L4–S1); obturator (L3–L4); piriformis (S1–S2)

cards.front: Test position for Hip external rotation against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, knees bent over the edge, towel under the distal thigh. Patient rotates so the foot moves inward, toward the other leg.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Hip external rotation?
cards.back: On the lateral distal thigh above the knee (counter-pressure).

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Hip external rotation?
cards.back: On the medial ankle, pushing the foot outward (toward internal rotation).

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Hip external rotation (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Supine: patient rolls the leg outward.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Deep — not reliably palpable.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Sartorius (hip flexion and abduction with knee flexion).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Gluteus minimus, anterior gluteus medius, tensor fasciae latae

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)

cards.front: Test position for Hip internal rotation against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, knees bent over the edge. Patient rotates so the foot moves outward.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: On the medial distal thigh.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: On the lateral ankle, pushing the foot inward (toward external rotation).

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Hip internal rotation (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Supine: patient rolls the leg inward.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: TFL just below and lateral to the ASIS.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Hip adduction and lifting the pelvis on that side.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Knee flexion?
cards.back: Biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Knee flexion?
cards.back: Sciatic (L5–S2): tibial part to the medial hamstrings and long head of biceps; common fibular part to the short head

cards.front: Test position for Knee flexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Prone, legs straight, feet over the edge. Patient bends the knee to about 90° (tibia neutral for all hamstrings, rotated in for medial, out for lateral).

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Knee flexion?
cards.back: On the back of the thigh/pelvis.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Knee flexion?
cards.back: On the back of the ankle, pulling toward extension.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Knee flexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Side-lying, test leg supported: patient slides the knee into flexion.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Knee flexion?
cards.back: Hamstring tendons behind the knee — biceps laterally, semitendinosus medially.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Knee flexion?
cards.back: Hip flexion (the pelvis lifts), sartorius/gracilis, gastrocnemius (ankle pulled up).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Knee extension?
cards.back: Quadriceps femoris

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Knee extension?
cards.back: Femoral nerve (L2–L4)

cards.front: Test position for Knee extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, knees bent over the edge, towel under the distal thigh, hands on the table. Patient straightens the knee without locking it.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Knee extension?
cards.back: On the distal thigh.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Knee extension?
cards.back: On the front of the leg above the ankle, pushing toward flexion.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Knee extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Side-lying, test leg supported: patient straightens the knee.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Knee extension?
cards.back: Quadriceps tendon above the patella or the patellar tendon.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Knee extension?
cards.back: Leaning back and hip internal rotation; locking the knee overestimates strength.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Gastrocnemius, soleus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Tibial nerve (S1–S2)

cards.front: Test position for Ankle plantarflexion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Standing on the test leg, fingertips on a wall for balance. Patient rises onto the toes (single-leg heel raise) through full range, repeatedly.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: None — the patient balances with fingertips only.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Body weight: grade 5 ≈ 20–25 consecutive full single-leg heel raises (editions of Daniels & Worthingham differ); fewer = grade 4; one full raise = grade 3.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Ankle plantarflexion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Prone with the foot over the edge (or side-lying): patient points the foot through range.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Achilles tendon and the gastrocnemius bellies.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Toe flexors (toes curl), tibialis posterior/peronei and leaning forward.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion?
cards.back: Tibialis anterior

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion?
cards.back: Deep fibular nerve (L4–L5)

cards.front: Test position for Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting, foot relaxed. Patient lifts the foot up and in, keeping the toes relaxed.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion?
cards.back: Behind the distal leg.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion?
cards.back: On the dorsomedial forefoot, pushing down and out.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Side-lying — grade by range (gravity has a small effect at the ankle).

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion?
cards.back: Tibialis anterior tendon on the front, inner ankle.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion?
cards.back: Toe extensors (EHL/EDL — the toes lift first).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Foot inversion?
cards.back: Tibialis posterior

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Foot inversion?
cards.back: Tibial nerve (L4–L5)

cards.front: Test position for Foot inversion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting (or side-lying on the test side), ankle slightly plantarflexed. Patient turns the sole inward.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Foot inversion?
cards.back: Above the ankle.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Foot inversion?
cards.back: On the medial forefoot, pushing toward eversion.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Foot inversion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Supine: patient inverts through range.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Foot inversion?
cards.back: Behind the medial malleolus.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Foot inversion?
cards.back: Tibialis anterior (adds dorsiflexion) and toe flexors.

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Foot eversion?
cards.back: Fibularis (peroneus) longus and brevis

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Foot eversion?
cards.back: Superficial fibular nerve (L5–S1)

cards.front: Test position for Foot eversion against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting (or side-lying on the untested side), ankle neutral. Patient turns the sole outward.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Foot eversion?
cards.back: Above the ankle.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Foot eversion?
cards.back: On the lateral border of the forefoot, pushing toward inversion.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Foot eversion (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Supine: patient everts through range.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Foot eversion?
cards.back: Behind and below the lateral malleolus; base of the 5th metatarsal.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Foot eversion?
cards.back: Extensor digitorum longus (eversion with dorsiflexion).

cards.front: Prime movers tested in Great toe extension?
cards.back: Extensor hallucis longus

cards.front: Nerve supply (roots) for Great toe extension?
cards.back: Deep fibular nerve (L5)

cards.front: Test position for Great toe extension against gravity (grades 3–5)?
cards.back: Sitting or supine, ankle neutral. Patient lifts the big toe up.

cards.front: Where do you stabilise when testing Great toe extension?
cards.back: Over the first metatarsal.

cards.front: Where, and in which direction, is resistance applied for Great toe extension?
cards.back: On the back of the big toe, pushing toward flexion.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for Great toe extension (grades 2 to 0)?
cards.back: Same position — grade by range.

cards.front: Where do you palpate for a grade 1 contraction in Great toe extension?
cards.back: EHL tendon on the back of the foot.

cards.front: Common substitution to watch for during Great toe extension?
cards.back: Ankle dorsiflexion.

cards.front: The patient lifts the arm through the full range against gravity but cannot hold against any resistance. Grade?
cards.back: 3. Full range against gravity with no added resistance is grade 3 (Fair).

cards.front: What does grade 2 (Poor) mean?
cards.back: Full range with gravity minimised. Grade 2 = full range only when gravity is minimised (horizontal plane).

cards.front: “Hold — don't let me move you” describes which method?
cards.back: Break test. In a break test the patient holds and the examiner gradually tries to break the hold.

cards.front: Which grade do you check first in a standard MMT?
cards.back: Grade 3 — full range against gravity. Test against gravity first; then go up with resistance or down to gravity-minimised positions.

cards.front: Grade 1 (Trace) means…
cards.back: Contraction felt or seen without joint movement. Trace = visible or palpable contraction with no movement of the joint.

cards.front: Why always test the other side too?
cards.back: Normal strength varies with age, size and dominance — the other side is the best reference. Comparison with the unaffected side is the most useful reference for 'normal' in that person.

cards.front: Resisted testing should be avoided over…
cards.back: An unhealed fracture of that segment. Resistance over an unhealed fracture risks displacement — follow medical clearance.

cards.front: MMT grades are least valid in which patient?
cards.back: Spasticity after a stroke. With spasticity, tone and synergy dominate movement; describe selective control and function instead.

cards.front: Where should resistance be applied?
cards.back: At the distal end of the moving segment, without crossing another joint. A distal point gives a long lever; crossing a second joint brings other muscles into the test.

cards.front: The main purpose of stabilisation is to…
cards.back: Isolate the movement and prevent substitution. Fixing the proximal segment isolates the tested muscle group.

cards.front: During side-lying hip abduction the leg drifts forward. Which muscle is substituting?
cards.back: Tensor fasciae latae (hip flexor-abductor). Drifting into flexion lets TFL and the hip flexors lift the leg — keep the hip slightly extended.

cards.front: How should resistance be built up?
cards.back: Gradually over 2–3 seconds, then held. Smooth build-up gives a fair, safe and repeatable test.

cards.front: Elbow flexion with the forearm pronated emphasises…
cards.back: Brachialis. Pronation puts biceps (a supinator) at a disadvantage, so brachialis does most of the work.

cards.front: Which note is correctly documented?
cards.back: R shoulder abduction 4/5, pain at end range; L 5/5. State side, movement, grade, comparison and modifiers such as pain.

cards.front: Why ask the patient not to lock the knee in the knee-extension test?
cards.back: A locked knee is held by joint position, overestimating quadriceps strength. Test just short of full extension so the muscle, not the locked joint, holds.

cards.front: A complete lower-limb screen is fastest when you…
cards.back: Group tests by patient position. Sitting → supine → side-lying → prone keeps position changes to a minimum.

cards.front: In the common convention, 3− means…
cards.back: More than half, but not all, of the range against gravity. 3− = more than half the range against gravity.

cards.front: Between which grades is MMT least reliable?
cards.back: 4 and 5. Examiners disagree most at the top of the scale — use dynamometry when it matters.

cards.front: The best tool to quantify strength above grade 4 objectively is…
cards.back: A handheld dynamometer. Dynamometers give a force value and reduce the ceiling effect.

cards.front: Fingers straighten before the wrist during wrist-extension testing. This is…
cards.back: Substitution by the finger extensors. Keep the fingers relaxed so the wrist extensors work alone.

cards.front: A positive Froment's sign shows weakness of…
cards.back: Adductor pollicis (ulnar nerve). The thumb IP flexes (FPL) to compensate for a weak adductor pollicis.

cards.front: Gravity-minimised position for knee extension?
cards.back: Side-lying with the test leg supported. Side-lying moves the knee in the horizontal plane.

cards.front: To test soleus rather than gastrocnemius, the knee should be…
cards.back: Flexed. Knee flexion slackens the two-joint gastrocnemius (active insufficiency).

cards.front: No movement, but you feel a contraction of the tendon when the patient tries. Grade?
cards.back: 1. A palpable contraction without movement is grade 1 (Trace).

cards.front: After a fall onto the shoulder: deltoid 2/5, a numb patch over the lateral upper arm, biceps 5/5 with a normal biceps reflex. — Most likely lesion?
cards.back: Axillary nerve injury. A C5 root or upper trunk lesion would also weaken biceps and change the reflex; isolated deltoid + 'regimental badge' numbness = axillary nerve.

cards.front: A 55-year-old has difficulty rising from chairs and lifting the arms overhead. Hips and shoulders 3+/5 on both sides, sensation and reflexes normal. — Which category of weakness fits best?
cards.back: Myopathy (proximal, symmetrical). Proximal symmetrical weakness with normal sensation and reflexes points to muscle disease.

cards.front: Strength is 5/5 on first testing but drops to 3/5 after ten repetitions; the patient describes drooping eyelids by evening. — What should you suspect?
cards.back: Neuromuscular junction disorder (e.g. myasthenia gravis). Fatigable weakness is the hallmark of NMJ disease — refer medically.

cards.front: EHL 3/5, hip abduction 4/5, ankle inversion 4/5, numbness over the dorsum of the foot and a reduced medial hamstring reflex. — Most likely site?
cards.back: L5 nerve root. Weak hip abductors (superior gluteal) and tibialis posterior (tibial) — both L5 but outside the fibular nerve — localise to the root.

cards.front: Foot drop after sitting cross-legged for hours: dorsiflexion 1/5, eversion 2/5, inversion 5/5, hip abduction 5/5, numb first web space and dorsum of the foot. — Most likely lesion?
cards.back: Common fibular nerve compression at the fibular head. Normal inversion (tibial) and hip abduction (superior gluteal) exclude the L5 root; the fibular nerve is compressed at the fibular head.

cards.front: Resisted shoulder abduction is 5/5 but reproduces the patient's lateral shoulder pain. — What does 'strong and painful' suggest?
cards.back: A minor lesion of the contractile tissue (e.g. tendinopathy). Strong and painful = contractile tissue lesion; weak and painless = neurological or complete rupture (Cyriax).

cards.front: Winging of the medial border of the scapula appears when the patient pushes against a wall; shoulder flexion is weak beyond 90°. — Which nerve should you suspect?
cards.back: Long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior). Medial winging with protraction = serratus anterior weakness from long thoracic nerve injury.

cards.front: Wrist drop with weak finger and thumb extension; elbow extension and the triceps reflex are normal; numb first dorsal web space. — Where is the radial nerve lesion?
cards.back: Spiral groove of the humerus (below the triceps branches). Triceps spared + wrist drop + sensory loss = spiral groove; PIN lesions spare sensation and wrist extension (ECRL).

cards.front: What is the maximum ISNCSCI total motor score?
cards.back: 100. 10 key muscles × grade 5 × 2 sides = 100.

cards.front: Six weeks after a stroke: elbow flexors 4/5 but the arm moves in a flexion synergy and tone is increased. — How should you report upper-limb motor function?
cards.back: Describe tone, synergy and selective motor control (e.g. Fugl-Meyer) rather than MMT alone. MMT assumes selective control; in UMN lesions use measures of motor control and function.

cards.front: Cervical flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Deep neck flexor endurance is tested separately (craniocervical flexion test); weakness is common after whiplash.

cards.front: Trunk flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Avoid loaded trunk flexion in osteoporosis or acute disc pain — choose another test.

cards.front: Scapular abduction & upward rotation — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Medial winging with weak serratus anterior = long thoracic nerve injury (heavy shoulder loads, axillary surgery).

cards.front: Scapular elevation — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Drooping shoulder and lateral winging with weak trapezius = spinal accessory nerve injury (e.g. after neck lymph-node surgery).

cards.front: Shoulder abduction — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Weak abduction + numb lateral arm + weak biceps = C5 root; weak deltoid + 'regimental badge' numbness with normal biceps = axillary nerve (e.g. after shoulder dislocation).

cards.front: Elbow flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Elbow flexion is the ISNCSCI key muscle for C5.

cards.front: Elbow extension — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Elbow extension is the ISNCSCI key muscle for C7.

cards.front: Wrist flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: FCU weakness appears with ulnar nerve lesions at the elbow; FCR with median lesions above the wrist.

cards.front: Wrist extension — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Wrist extension is the ISNCSCI key muscle for C6; wrist drop = radial nerve palsy (mid-shaft humerus fracture, 'Saturday-night palsy').

cards.front: Finger DIP flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: FDP of the middle finger is the ISNCSCI key muscle for C8.

cards.front: Finger abduction — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Little-finger abduction (abductor digiti minimi) is the ISNCSCI key muscle for T1.

cards.front: Thumb palmar abduction — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Weak APB with thenar wasting = median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel).

cards.front: Thumb adduction — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: A positive Froment's sign signals ulnar nerve weakness of adductor pollicis.

cards.front: Hip flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Hip flexion is the ISNCSCI key muscle for L2.

cards.front: Hip abduction — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Weak gluteus medius produces a Trendelenburg sign; think superior gluteal nerve or the L5 root.

cards.front: Knee extension — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Knee extension is the ISNCSCI key muscle for L3.

cards.front: Ankle plantarflexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Ankle plantarflexion is the ISNCSCI key muscle for S1; non-weight-bearing manual testing underestimates calf weakness.

cards.front: Ankle dorsiflexion & inversion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Ankle dorsiflexion is the ISNCSCI key muscle for L4; foot drop = common/deep fibular nerve or L4–L5 root.

cards.front: Great toe extension — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Great toe extension is the ISNCSCI key muscle for L5.
